What does Manton say about how a believer’s experience of God’s grace influences their desire for further communion with Him?

Manton teaches that tasting the Lord’s graciousness creates a yearning for more intimate fellowship. He explains that once a believer has "tasted that the Lord is gracious," this experience "kindles affection, and makes us long for more," leading to a renewed resolution to serve the Lord more faithfully and to walk in holiness. He further notes that "When you find benefit by one duty, it will be an encouragement to come again," indicating that each encounter with divine grace fuels a deeper desire for continued communion. [Manton — Works Vol14]

What does the sermon say about the responsibility of God's people in seeking the salvation of souls and the consequences of failing to do so?

Spurgeon teaches that believers are accountable for earnestly seeking the salvation of souls, warning that neglect brings severe accountability. He states, "if you who are His people are not earnest in seeking the salvation of souls, and they perish, their blood will be required at your hands!" The sermon underscores that while God’s sovereign will ultimately prevails, human earnestness in prayer and evangelism is essential; otherwise, the consequences fall upon the neglectful believers, as illustrated by the example of King Joash deciding whether the Syrians should be beaten three or six times. [Sermon 2303 — "Three Arrows--or Six?"]

What financial advantage does Cotton Mather claim the abolition of Popery would bring to England?

Mather argues that abolishing Popery would be a great economic benefit, noting that “the Abolifhing of Popery in England, is worth at Leaft Eight Millions of Pounds yearly to the Nation.” He presents this as a monetary incentive for embracing the Protestant religion. [Cotton Mather — Bonifacius Essays To Do Good]

According to Gill, how does God's providence relate to natural and necessary actions?

Gill teaches that the providence of God is concerned in all actions, "from the beginning to the end of it," and that He is a "God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed" (1 Sam. 2:3). He explains that every muscular motion—such as birds flying, fish swimming, and humans walking—is continued by God's providence, because all motion ultimately comes from the first Mover, "in whom we live, and move, and have our being" (Acts 17:28). Gill further distinguishes that necessary actions either arise from the necessity of nature or are appointed by God's ordination. This shows that both natural activities and those required by nature are under divine governance. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

What covenantal promise does Gill describe regarding believers being adopted as children of God?

Gill teaches that the covenant includes a promise that believers "should be openly adopted, and declared the children of God," meaning that God will treat them as His own offspring, granting them the status of His people, heirs, and portion. This adoption signifies a relational bond whereby God becomes their Father and they become His children, receiving both the discipline of the covenant rod and the inheritance promised to His people. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

According to Witsius in the Economy of the Covenants, how many appearances of God to Abraham are recorded?

Witsius states that the scriptural record shows that "the scriptures testify, that God appeared eight times to Abraham." He includes this detail as part of his brief overview of the appearances made to Abraham and the covenant that followed, emphasizing its role in the doctrine of grace from Abraham to Moses. According to the 1708 sermon, what are the three distinct ways the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers?

The sermon explains that the Holy Spirit convicts and empowers believers in a threefold manner. First, He is described as “the Holy Spirit was to be their Comforter, that they might not be afraid,” providing comfort and courage. Second, He serves as “their Advocate, that they might not be baffled,” defending and guiding them. Third, He operates as a divine power in communication: “When they spoke, there would be a power within them suggesting their words, a power with those words convincing their hearers, and a power in their hearers causing the word spoken to abide in their memories.” In this way the Spirit works within the speaker, persuades the listener, and secures the spoken word in memory. [Sermon 1708 — "The Holy Spirit's Threefold Conviction of Men"]

Why does Manton argue that one must not delay the work of saving one's soul until later in life?

Manton teaches that a person must begin the work of salvation immediately because "death comes by way of surprise; it finds us before we look for it," and postponing it leads to grief when one is too weak to bear it. He warns that waiting until the appointed time "to think of saving our souls" is foolish, likening it to a traveller who sets out at night or the foolish virgins who bought oil too late. The urgency is rooted in the belief that we are sent into the world for "our trial and for our exercise," not for idle pleasure. [Manton — Works Vol16]

What are the threefold subordination of Christ that Hodge identifies in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 3:23‑63?

Hodge explains that “the Scriptures speak of a threefold subordination of Christ.” He outlines the three aspects as follows: (1) “A subordination as to the mode of subsistence and operation, of the second, to the first person in the Trinity,” which maintains the unity of substance while distinguishing roles; (2) “the voluntary subordination of the Son in his humbling himself to be found in fashion as a man, and becoming obedient unto death,” indicating Christ’s self‑limitation in incarnation; and (3) “the economical or official subjection of the theanthropos,” referring to Christ’s functional role in the redemptive administration. [Hodge — Commentary 1Corinthians]

What does the sermon warn about using encouragements to believe as a 'halfway house' before true faith?

Spurgeon warns that treating encouragements to believe as a provisional resting place is dangerous, stating that "If encouragements to believe are used as a sort of halfway house to rest in before actually believing, they are mischievously used and may ruin our souls!" He illustrates the peril by contrasting this with the example of the afflicted woman who, out of genuine confidence in Christ, pressed directly to the Savior’s garment and was healed. The sermon emphasizes that true faith, not mere encouragement, brings wholeness, and that after such healing a period of fear may follow as a natural response to the joy of salvation. [Sermon 3020 — "Good Cheer From Grace Received"]

According to the 1689 Second London Confession, what happened to Christ after his death and before His resurrection?

The 1689 Second London Confession teaches that after Christ’s crucifixion He "remained in the state of the dead, yet saw no corruption" and that "on the third day he arose from the dead with the same body in which he suffered". It further states that He ascended into heaven, now sits at the right hand of the Father, intercedes for believers, and will return to judge men and angels at the end of the world. [1689 — Second London Confession]

What does Spurgeon say about how God protects Christ’s fame against blasphemy and rebellion in Sermon 3436?

Spurgeon teaches that, although Christ is blasphemed by rebels, dishonored by apostates, and grieved by humanity, God will not allow His fame to be tarnished even for a moment. He emphasizes that God has declared, "He has glorified You," and that the Father has exalted the Son with a name above every name that will never be second. Moreover, Spurgeon declares that "God has glorified Him in the entire economy of salvation," ensuring that the crown remains safe upon Christ’s head despite the nations’ rebellion. [Sermon 3436 — "Christ Glorified"]

How does Manton explain the changing ways in which God is near to His people?

Manton teaches that God’s nearness is not constant in the same manner, but varies according to divine purpose and human experience. He writes that God is “nearer to us sometimes than at others, when we have more evidences of his favour inward or outward,” describing inward evidences as moments when He “quickens, comforts, supports the soul, filleth the heart with joy and peace in believing.” Conversely, he notes that outwardly “sometimes God hideth himself, some times seemeth not to mind the affairs of his people, at other times all the world shall know that they are near and dear to him.” Manton also affirms that while God “is not alike always present with his people, but never withdraweth that influence that is necessary to the being of grace,” He remains ever‑present in a sustaining way. This dynamic picture shows that God’s presence can be felt both in hidden and manifest forms, according to His good pleasure. [Manton — Works Vol09]

According to Spurgeon in Sermon 1064, how is merit treated in the doctrine of salvation?

Spurgeon teaches that merit has no place in the Christian Church and that all salvation is received solely by God’s free favor. He declares that “Merit is an unknown word in the Christian Church--it is banished once and for all” and emphasizes that every blessing comes through grace, not human achievement. Consequently, boasting is excluded because “not of works, lest any man should boast.” In this view the Apostle’s declaration, “By Grace are you saved, through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God; not of works, lest any man should boast,” underscores that salvation is a gift, not a merit‑based reward. [Sermon 1064 — "Salvation All of Grace"]

Why does Calvin describe Abraham as "the father of all them that believe" in his commentary on Galatians and Ephesians?

Calvin teaches that Abraham exemplifies the principle of justification by faith, showing that righteousness comes solely through belief and not works. He points out that Scripture declares "the same are the children of Abraham" and that there is "no variety of roads to righteousness," so Abraham serves as the universal pattern for all believers. Because God justified Abraham on the basis of his faith, Calvin concludes that Abraham is rightly called "the father of all them that believe," (Romans 4:11) and his example establishes the rule for obtaining righteousness for every nation. [Calvin — Commentary Galatians Ephesians]

What does Perkins’ Golden Chain say are the two parts of the sacramental word, and what roles do they play in a sacrament?

Perkins explains that the sacramentall word consists of two distinct elements: the commandment and the promise. He writes, "The sacramentall word, is the word of institution, the which God after a seuerall manner, hath set downe in each Sacrament." The commandment is the directive by which Christ appoints the administration of the sacrament and the receiving of it, as illustrated in Baptism (“Go into the whole world baptizing them in the Name…”) and the Lord’s Supper (“Take, eat, drink, doe ye this”). The promise, on the other hand, is the assurance that the ordained elements serve as instruments and seals of divine grace, exemplified by the baptismal formula “I baptize thee in the name of the father, of the sonne, and of the holy Ghost.” Thus, the commandment governs the outward act, while the promise secures the inward grace. [Perkins — Golden Chain]

What does Edwards say about the reliability of people’s hearts in attaining heaven?

Edwards teaches that many who profess confidence in their own salvation are in fact vulnerable to backsliding and cannot be relied upon to reach heaven, because "the hearts of men are very unsteady; they are not to be trusted." He warns that even those who seem engaged may lose grace when temptations arise, and that without true divine assistance they will be "soon discouraged" and fall into the "fiery billows of God's wrath." [Edwards — Sermons Worcester Vol8]

What does the sermon say is necessary to 'lay hold on eternal life' and how is this connected to 'fight the good fight of the faith'?

The sermon teaches that laying hold on eternal life is not a passive or dreamy pursuit; it requires the believer’s utmost energy, personal effort, and the Divine assistance that comes through faith. It stresses that one must "fight the good fight of the faith" by personally possessing the inward life and displaying its power in daily conduct, rather than relying on mere reasoning or scholarly arguments. In other words, the two commands—"fight the good fight of the faith" and "lay hold on eternal life"—are inseparably linked, demanding active, faith‑driven struggle to obtain and live out the divine life. [Sermon 1946 — "Eternal Life Within Present Grasp"]

What does Gurnall say about the insufficiency of moral uprightness that lacks the aim of God's glory?

Gurnall teaches that moral uprightness that is not directed toward the glory of God is merely a partial virtue and therefore falls short of true uprightness. He explains that a person may act faithfully toward an earthly master, yet "God never looked at, or thought of, in all this, and so all worth nothing, because God is left out of the story." The ultimate purpose, he asserts, is to do everything "to the glory of God," quoting 1 Cor. X. 31, "Whatever ye do, do all to the glory of God." Moreover, he cites Eph. vi. 7 that servants must "do their service as to God, not to man;" thus the chief end of any duty is the glorification of God, not merely human approval. [Gurnall — Christian In Complete Armour]

According to Owen, what are the consequences of omitting the first intention of the law and proceeding “per saltum” to the latter?

Owen argues that skipping the first intention of the law and moving “per saltum,” to the latter, turns a law that was “designed for the good of all men” into “the danger of all and ruin of many.” He explains that this practice “takes away all security of their goods and estates” from peaceable subjects, allowing “every evil man … to take the goods of other men into his own possession” while the owner remains unaware of the cause. Consequently, the legal right to one’s own property is transferred to another, who is then enabled by force to keep it, undermining the principal end of the law to secure each person’s possession of his goods until a lawful conviction. [Owen — Works Vol13]

What metaphors does Swinnock employ to illustrate how ungodly men deceive and prey upon Christians?

Swinnock depicts ungodly men as employing a series of deceptive images: they are "about me like Bees, with honey in their mouths and a sting in their tails"; they act "as Butchers, they claw the Ox about the ribs, that they may have the fairer blow at his head"; and he likens them to a pelican that "swalloweth shell‑fish, and warmeth them in her stomach, but it is to make them gape, that she may pick them out of the shels (where they are safe whilst they are shut) and devour them." By using these vivid analogies, Swinnock warns that such men appear sweet or harmless while secretly preparing to trap and devour believers. [Swinnock — Works 1665]

Spurgeon teaches that the initial method of ‘Come and see’ is by observation. He urges believers to “give attention to the teaching of the Gospel, to weigh it and prove it.” If the message proves false it must be cast away, but if it is found worthy it should be held fast and never let go. Why does the sermon say that many believers fail to recognize the Holy Spirit as a person?

The sermon teaches that the difficulty stems from habit and language: believers are so accustomed to speaking of the Holy Ghost’s influence and operations that they "have acquired the habit of regarding the Holy Ghost as an emanation flowing from the Father and the Son, but not as being actually a person himself." Consequently, they tend to view the Spirit as a mere emanation rather than a true subsistence, one person in the essence of the Godhead. [Sermon 4 — "The Personality of the Holy Ghost"]

According to Bayly’s ‘Practice Of Piety’, what are the six specific purposes for observing a baptism with reverent attention?

Bayly teaches that when baptism is to be administered the observer should stay and behold it with reverent attention for six distinct purposes. First, the believer must “First, Shew thy reverence to God's ordinance;” thereby honoring the divine command. Second, one should consider “the better consider thine own ingrafting into the visible body of Christ's church,” reflecting on personal incorporation into the body of Christ. Third, the observer is to “repay thy debts, in praying for the infant which is to be baptized,” interceding that God grants the infant the inward effects of baptism. Fourth, the faithful should “assist the church in praising God for grafting another member into his mystical body,” joining the corporate worship. Fifth, the believer is to “prove whether the effects of Christ's death killeth sin in thee, and whether thou be raised to newness of life by the virtue of his resurrection,” examining the transformative power of the gospel. Sixth, one must “show thyself to be a freeman of Christ's corporation, having a voice or consent in the admission of others into that holy society,” affirming a participatory role in the church. These six purposes together shape a reverent and reflective posture toward baptism. [Bayly — Practice Of Piety]

How does Edwards differentiate between God's perceptive will and His disposing will when explaining the sincerity of divine commands, counsels, and invitations?

Edwards argues that the sincerity of God's commands, counsels, and invitations is grounded in what he calls God's perceptive will, not in a deterministic disposing will. He explains that even if events are ordained as necessary, God can still “sincerely command and require” man to act, because such commands flow from the perceptive will that reflects what God loves and what is agreeable to the human heart. As he puts it, "Counsels and invitations are manifestations of God's perceptive will, or of what God loves, and what is in itself, and as man's act, agreeable to his heart ; and not of his disposing will, and what he chooses as a part of his own infinite scheme of things." Thus, divine commands remain sincere and genuine, despite any underlying necessity. [Edwards — Freedom Of The Will]

Calvin explains that natural perspicacity, the liberal arts, and all sciences are inherently "gifts of God." However, he clarifies that these gifts are confined within their own limits and "cannot penetrate" into God's heavenly kingdom. If they set themselves in opposition to Christ, they are to be regarded as dangerous pests and hindrances. How does Howe illustrate the soul's capacity to act independently of corporeal organs?

Howe illustrates the soul's capacity to act independently of corporeal organs by explaining that the soul's very use of these organs implies an action antecedent to their assistance. He posits that the soul "supposes an operation upon them, antecedent to any operation by them." As an example, he notes that when one uses a pen, one first acts upon it to impress motion, an action that does not itself require another instrument. This suggests that the soul's action upon an organ must ultimately occur without the ministry of any organ, to avoid an infinite regress of bodies. Furthermore, Howe argues that even when separated from the body, the soul is not diminished but can still "perform those operations, which are proper to it self; that is, such as are more noble, and excellent, and immediately conducive to its own felicitie." He compares the soul's inability to perform "meaner, and grosser pieces of drudgerie" out of the body to a magistrate not personally executing a malefactor, emphasizing that this does not signify disparagement or diminution of its proper functions.
[Howe — Blessedness Of The Righteous]

Spurgeon highlights a stark contrast between the simple, truthful understanding of God's active involvement in creation, as taught in childhood, and the complex, God-excluding theories prevalent in a 'proudly enlightened age.' He recounts how mothers taught children, through hymns like Watts', that "My God, who makes the sun to know His proper hour to rise, And to give light to all below, Does send him round the skies." This truth, he argues, is being challenged by modern "schools of philosophy and science" that are "spinning all sorts of theories to get rid of God, to turn our Benefactor out of His own world and put man's best Friend as far away as possible." Spurgeon suggests that these skeptical teachers would benefit from returning to a simpler faith, recognizing that "our heavenly Father 'makes His sun to rise and He sends the rain,'" and that "Laws of Nature can do nothing without a power at the back of the laws."
[Sermon 1414 — "No Difference"]

Spurgeon describes a Christian who has lost the brightness of his evidences as one who looks on the past with pleasure, the future with dread, and the present with sorrow. [Sermon 51 — "Comfort for the Desponding"]

According to Owen, what is the means by which believers obtain a right to God's inheritance?

Owen teaches that a believer’s right to the inheritance is secured not by any portion of creation but by an interest in Christ and union with Him, which is effected through the participation of the Spirit of Christ. He explains that the Spirit of adoption makes believers children of God, and as children they become heirs: "If we are children, then heirs, heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ." Consequently, the inheritance is received by free, gratuitous adoption, making believers joint heirs with Christ. [Owen — Works Vol04]

How does Owen explain the way God adapts His self‑descriptions to human understanding?

Owen explains that God does not alter His essence when speaking to humanity, but rather He "condescendeth to accommodate his ways and proceedings" to human apprehensions. He stresses that this accommodation does not mean God "speaks one thing and intends the clean contrary," but that the divine attributes are expressed in terms that suit our limited perception, such as saying that "his eyes run to and fro, to behold the sons of men" even though God has no fleshly eyes. Thus, the language used is meant to convey divine perfection in a manner understandable to people, not to suggest any inconsistency in God's nature. [Owen — Works Vol12]

What does Gill say about the fate of the law in relation to the biblical statements that heaven and earth will pass away?

Gill teaches that the Scriptures affirm that the moral law will never be nullified, even though the created order is temporary. He notes that the first of those scriptures only says, "till heaven and earth pass", which will never be; and so not one jot or tittle of the law shall pass till all be fulfilled. Thus, while "heaven and earth shall pass away", the law endures until its ultimate fulfillment, and the passing of the world refers only to the temporary fashion and lusts of the age, not to the divine moral decree. [Systematic — Gill Body Of Doctrinal Divinity]

Spurgeon teaches that every individual will experience two distinct advents. He writes, "Every man will have two advents--the advent which he now enjoys or which he now misuses upon earth--and the advent which lies beyond the present course of probation." According to Spurgeon in Sermon 660, how does the Holy Spirit bring spiritual light to humanity?

Spurgeon teaches that humanity is "dark, dark, dark" and dwells in the black darkness of sin until the Holy Spirit renews it, granting the "true Light which lights every man which comes into the world." He points out that no one has even a spark of spiritual light unless it is received from above, and that the Spirit’s work begins mysteriously in the heart. Spurgeon illustrates this mystery with the image: "The wind blows where it wishes and you hear the sound of it, but cannot tell from where it comes and where it goes: so is everyone that is born of the Spirit." He also recalls the first divine act of creation, "The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters," as a prefigure of the Spirit’s renewing power. In this way, the Holy Spirit silently and efficaciously quickens the dead heart, excites emotions, longings, and desires, bringing spiritual illumination to those chosen. [Sermon 660 — "Light--Natural And Spiritual"]

Which early church fathers does Aa Hodge cite as supporting infant baptism as an apostolic tradition?

In Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology, Hodge records that several early Christian writers affirm infant baptism as an apostolic tradition. He notes that Justin Martyr (a.d. 138) says, "There were among Christians of his time, many persons of both sexes, some sixty and some seventy years old, who had been made disciples of Christ from their infancy." Irenaeus (born about a.d. 97) declares that "He came to save all by himself; all I say who by him are born again unto God, infants, and little children and youths." Origen (a.d. 185) observes that it was "the usage of the church to baptize infants," and adds that "the church had received the tradition from the apostles." Cyprian (bishop of Carthage, a.d. 248‑258) and his synod mandated infant baptism before the eighth day, and Augustine (a.d. 358) affirms that this "doctrine is held by the whole church, not instituted by councils, but always retained." Thus Hodge presents a continuous patristic witness to infant baptism as apostolic. [Systematic — Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology]

What two conditions does Hodge say Roman Catholic theology requires for a sacrament to be efficacious?

Hodge explains that Roman Catholic teaching holds the efficacy of a sacrament on the part of the administrator to two essential conditions. First, the minister must be "canonically authorized"—for the sacraments of orders and confirmation he must be a bishop in communion with the pope, and for the other sacraments he must be a regular popish priest; the personal character of the bishop or priest, even if he be in mortal sin, does not prevent the effect. Second, the minister must exercise the positive intention to do what the church intends, because "To the valid performance of the sacrament is required the intention upon the part of the officiating minister of doing that which the church does." [Systematic — Aa Hodge Outlines Of Theology]

How does Sibbes explain the presence of lingering sin after a person has received pardon?

Sibbes teaches that even after pardon the root of sin may still linger like the dregs of a disease, because sanctification proceeds gradually and each prayer and renewal of repentance carries away some of the debt until the final physician—death—perfectly cures both soul and body. What reason does Edwards give for why fore‑known events must actually exist, based on God's immutable knowledge?

Edwards argues that because God's knowledge is immutable, it cannot change or be succeeded by a new view; therefore any event that God foreknows cannot fail to exist. He explains that "the immutability of knowledge makes his knowledge to be without succession" and concludes that "it is utterly impossible the known events should fail of existence." Since a failure would require a change in God's knowledge, which is impossible, the existence of fore‑known events is guaranteed. [Edwards — Freedom Of The Will]

What does Calvin say is present in the Lord's Supper, and how does the Reformed view of the mode of reception differ from the Lutheran view?

Calvin teaches that the presence in the Lord's Supper is not the natural body and blood of Christ but "a supernatural, life-giving influence emanating from his glorified body in heaven, and conveyed to the believer by the power of the Holy Ghost." The Reformed position holds that the mode of reception is spiritual, with "the organ is not the mouth, but faith," and the condition of reception is the presence and exercise of faith, contrasting with the Lutheran view that the body and blood are received "corporaliter" through the mouth and actual consumption of the elements. [Systematic — Systematic Theology Vol3]

What eight supports does Brooks provide for believers who have lost assurance?

Brooks outlines eight biblical supports for those who have lost assurance. The first is that “the great God might have burnt up all, he might not have left one house standing.” The second support is "That God has given them their lives for a prey." The third points to the common lot of sinners and saints. The fourth declares that even though believers have lost much as citizens, merchants, and tradesmen, they have lost nothing as “Cliristians, as they are saints, as they are the called of God.” The fifth assures that the Lord will certainly make up all their losses. The sixth promises that by fiery dispensations the Lord will make way for the new heavens and the new earth and the glorious deliverance of his people. The seventh foretells that God will bring about the ruin and destruction of his and his people's enemies. The eighth concludes that all shall end well and all shall work for good. [Brooks — Complete Works Vol6]

What does Ambrose say is the purpose of Christ’s ascension and sitting at the right hand of God?

Ambrose teaches that Christ’s ascent was not an end in itself but a preparation for the work of dispensing divine blessings to the saints. He explains that after rising, “Christ is gone up to heaven, Christ is set down at God's right hand,” where He is “invested with all the riches of Heaven” and holds “all the keyes of Heaven and Hell.” From that position He “gave gifts unto men, yea, he gave the gift of gifts, even the Holy Ghost himself,” so that believers may partake of that Spirit. Thus the purpose of the ascension is to enable Christ to bestow the Holy Spirit and all heavenly riches upon His people. [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]

Why does Ambrose claim that seeking earthly comforts is ultimately futile?

Ambrose teaches that the pursuit of earthly comforts is futile because the earth is a place of sorrow, trouble, and mourning rather than lasting pleasure. He asks, "Oh why do we seek the living among the dead?" to illustrate the emptiness of seeking life in a world destined for death, and he contrasts the fleeting joys of the wicked with the eternal reward promised to the godly. [Ambrose — Looking Unto Jesus]

What mistake does Bolton identify regarding those who think prayer alone is sufficient for Christian duty?

Bolton identifies the error of believing that prayer alone fulfills all Christian obligations. According to Cartwright, does Christ’s coming aim to abolish existing civil government and its judicial laws?

Cartwright teaches that Christ’s mission was not to overturn established civil authority. He notes that "our Saviour Christ came not to dissolve any good Government of Common-wealth," and therefore Christ cannot be thought to destroy what He Himself established. Moreover, Cartwright argues that the judicial law remains binding, not merely as a counsel "they list, and leave at their pleasure," but as a law to which people are bound. This continuity of equity underlies the responsibility of Christian magistrates to frame political laws grounded in everlasting equity. [Cartwright — Helps For Discovery]

Spurgeon teaches that every single act of Jesus is not a trivial occurrence but a divine sign that conveys a wealth of instruction. How does Boyce describe the role of good works in the believer’s sanctification?

Boyce teaches that good works are a secondary means of sanctification, stating that "the good works of the Christian, furnish another secondary means for his sanctification." He clarifies that these works are not perfect in a legal sense, but are the outward actions that result from a life lived through the Spirit. Moreover, Boyce notes that "These good works are the result of sanctification ; but, in their performance, they naturally become the means of further sanctification," indicating that while they flow from prior sanctification, they also serve to deepen it when performed in connection with the truth of God. [Systematic — Boyce Abstract Of Systematic Theology]

How does Sibbes characterize the dominant preaching style of his era in Works Vol01?

Sibbes observes that the dominant preaching of his era had become a "frivolous, florid eloquence, that boasted itself on its deftly-turned tropes, its high-flown paraphrases of the classics, especially Seneca and Cicero, and the Fathers," likening the multiplied quotations to "purple patches on a thread-bare robe" and suggesting that such mannered discourse was merely a superficial display lacking true spiritual substance. [Sibbes — Works Vol01]

What threefold fullness of Christ does Goodwin describe, and how does he connect the church to this fullness?

Goodwin teaches that Christ possesses a personal fullness—the fullness of the Godhead dwelling personally in him—, a dispensatory fullness, in which he "filleth all in all." and from which believers receive grace for grace, and a relative fullness that arises from his relation to the church. He explains that the church is an “empty vessel” that displays his fullness, echoing "My strength is made perfect in weakness." [Goodwin — Works Vol01]

What does the Institutes Beveridge Vol2 say about the fate of hypocritical believers who pretend piety?

The Institutes explain that Christ declares that hypocrites who pretend piety will ultimately be removed from the place they improperly occupy, noting the Psalm question “ Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle ? who shall dwell in thy holy hill ?” as a prophetic illustration. The work also distinguishes between election to an office and election to salvation, observing that although Judas was chosen as an apostle, he is excluded from the elect, as the passage records “I speak not of you all : I know whom I have chosen,”. [Institutes — Institutes Beveridge Vol2]

According to Sermon 1429, what biblical passage does Spurgeon cite as the foundation of faith and how does he describe its significance?

Spurgeon teaches that the sure foundation of faith is found in Isaiah 28:16, which he quotes verbatim: "Therefore thus says the Lord God, behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious cornerstone, a sure foundation." He explains that this stone is the object of belief, noting that Paul interprets the promise as "shall not be ashamed" and Peter renders it "shall not be confounded," indicating that believers who trust in this cornerstone will never be disgraced or confused. The repeated citation of this verse by the apostle Paul underscores its central role in establishing a secure basis for Christian faith. [Sermon 1429 — "Faith's Sure Foundation"]

What two lessons does Spurgeon say we learn from the seed that falls by the wayside in his sermon "The Seed by the Wayside"?

Spurgeon teaches that believers must recognize that not all efforts bear fruit; he says, "As he sowed, some fell by the wayside; and it was trodden down, and the fowls of the air devoured it," and concludes that we learn two truths: first, we shall have some unprofitable labors, and second, some soils will remain unsuitable for the Good Seed. [Sermon 2843 — "The Seed by the Wayside"]

What does Manton advise a child of God to do regarding worldly possessions and affections?

Manton teaches that a child of God should not be drawn to the fleeting pleasures of the world but should direct his heart toward eternal things. He urges believers to "Set your affections on things above, not on things in the earth," and to subordinate any earthly desire to heavenly priorities, avoiding competition with divine purposes. He also warns against acquiring wealth by unjust means, emphasizing that true happiness lies in the inheritance of God rather than in worldly honor or wealth. [Manton — Works Vol08]

According to Sermon 392, what does the author say is the true source of wisdom and how can it be obtained?

According to the Greenham work, how does the author describe the value of circumcision versus becoming a new creature in Christ?

The author of the Greenham work declares that in Christ "neither circumcision auaileth any thing, nor vncircumcision, but a new creature." By emphasizing this, the writer argues that external rites such as circumcision have no merit compared with the transformative reality of being a new creature through the cross of Jesus, echoing Paul’s protest that true boasting belongs to the cross alone. [Greenham — Works]

What does Sibbes mean by the ‘double comfort’ that God provides to believers?

Sibbes explains that the ‘double comfort’ consists of two linked assurances: first, God will raise believers out of present troubles, which he likens to a kind of death, and second, God will raise them out of the grave and present them before the Lord at the final judgment. He writes, "The comfort is double. God will raise us up, and then God will present us with you," indicating that the same power that raised Christ from the dead will also lift the faithful from both temporal afflictions and ultimate death, uniting them forever with Christ. [Sibbes — Works Vol04]
